## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: false
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).

R is widely used for statistical computing [@rmanual].

# Exercise 1

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(ggrepel)


```

```{r}
pisa <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "pisa_2022.csv"))
head(pisa)

## Plot 1

plot1_data <- pisa %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_math = mean(math, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_read = mean(read, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(plot1_data, aes(mean_math, mean_read)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = country)) +
  labs(
    title = "Average reading against average maths for each country",
    subtitle = "Any guesses on where Australia ranks?",
    x = "mean scores in mathematics",
    y = "mean scores in reading"
  )



## Plot 2

plot2_data <- pisa %>%
  group_by(country, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_math = mean(math, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_read = mean(read, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_sci = mean(science, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_math, mean_read, mean_sci),
    names_to = "subject",
    values_to = "mean_score"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = gender,
    values_from = mean_score
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    diff = female - male,
    `diff > 0` = diff > 0
  )

ggplot(plot2_data, aes(x = diff, y = country, colour = `diff > 0`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ subject, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average gender difference (diff = female - male) per Country",
    subtitle = "Gender gap in reading is universal, but math and science gaps are not.",
    x = "diff",
    y = "country",
    colour = "diff > 0"
  )
```

Plot 1 shows a strong positive relationship between mathematics and reading scores across countries. Countries with higher mathematics scores generally also achieve higher reading scores.

Plot 2 shows that female students generally outperform male students in reading across most countries, while differences in mathematics and science vary between countries.

# Exercise 2

```{r exercise-2, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(lubridate)

# Load datasets
house <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "aus_median_house_price.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

gdp <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "aus_GDP_changes.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Clean Melbourne median established house transfer price
melb_house <- house %>%
  select(
    Date = 1,
    Price = `Median Price of Established House Transfers (Unstratified) ;  Melbourne ;`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Date = parse_date_time(Date, orders = c("my", "bY", "Ymd")),
    Price = parse_number(as.character(Price))
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Date), !is.na(Price))

# Plot 1
ggplot(melb_house, aes(x = Date, y = Price)) +
  geom_line(colour = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Median Price of Established House Transfers in Melbourne",
    subtitle = "Unstratified & not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL,
    y = "A$ ('000)",
    caption = "Source: ABS"
  )

# Identify low GDP growth periods
gdp_low <- gdp %>%
  mutate(
    Date = as.Date(DATE),
    low_growth = GDP_changes < 0.1,
    in_house_time = Date >= min(melb_house$Date) & Date <= max(melb_house$Date)
  ) %>%
  filter(low_growth == TRUE, in_house_time == TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    xmin = Date - months(1),
    xmax = Date + months(1)
  )

gdp_low

ggplot(melb_house, aes(Date, Price)) +

geom_rect(
data = gdp_low,
aes(
xmin = xmin,
xmax = xmax,
ymin = -Inf,
ymax = Inf
),
fill = "grey70",
alpha = 0.5,
inherit.aes = FALSE
) +

geom_line(colour = "blue") +

labs(
title = "Median Price of Established House Transfers in Melbourne",
subtitle = "Unstratified & not seasonally adjusted",
x = NULL,
y = "A$ ('000)",
caption = "Shaded areas indicate GDP increased less than 0.1% at that quarter.\nSources: ABS."
) +
theme_minimal()


```

Plot 1 shows that Melbourne median established house transfer prices increased strongly over time, especially after 2015, with a clear peak around 2021–2022.

Plot 2 shows the same house price trend with shaded periods representing very low GDP growth. These shaded areas help compeconomic growth periods with changes in Melbourne house prices.

# Exercise 3

```{r exercise-3, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dbplyr)
library(here)

# Create temporary SQLite database
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")

# Load CSV files
actors <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "actors.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
castings <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "castings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
movies <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "movies.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
directors <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "directors.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Copy data into database
copy_to(con, actors, "actors", temporary = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)
copy_to(con, castings, "castings", temporary = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)
copy_to(con, movies, "movies", temporary = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)
copy_to(con, directors, "directors", temporary = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)

# Create database table references
actors_db <- tbl(con, "actors")
castings_db <- tbl(con, "castings")
movies_db <- tbl(con, "movies")
directors_db <- tbl(con, "directors")


## Part 1: Most common director–actor partnerships


director_actor_partnerships <- actors_db %>%
  left_join(castings_db, by = "ActorID") %>%
  left_join(movies_db, by = "MovieID") %>%
  left_join(directors_db, by = "DirectorID") %>%
  group_by(actor_name = Name.x, director_name = Name.y) %>%
  summarise(number_of_movies = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(number_of_movies))

director_actor_partnerships %>%
  head(10) %>%
  collect()



## Part 2: Translate the SQL query into dbplyr


actor_director_summary <- actors_db %>%
  left_join(castings_db, by = "ActorID") %>%
  left_join(movies_db, by = "MovieID") %>%
  left_join(directors_db, by = "DirectorID") %>%
  group_by(actor_name = Name.x) %>%
  summarise(
    unique_directors = n_distinct(Name.y),
    total_movies = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(unique_directors))

actor_director_summary %>%
  collect()

```

The first query identifies director–actor partnerships that appear most frequently in the movie database. A high count means that the same actor and director worked together across multiple movies.

The second query asks which actors have worked with the largest number of different directors. This can show actors with broad collaboration networks, while `total_movies` shows how many total movie records each actor has in the database.

# Exercise 4

This report is written as a High Distinction level attempt because it includes Pearson’s chi-squared test, Fisher’s exact test, and a simulation study comparing rejection rates across four settings.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Exercise 4

## Introduction

## This exercise compares two statistical methods used for analysing a 2-by-2     contingency table:

   ##- Pearson’s chi-squared test  
   ##- Fisher’s exact test  

##Both tests are used to examine whether two categorical variables are independent. In this example, the variables are:

   ##- Gender (Men / Women)
   ##- Study status (Studying / Not studying)

##We test whether the proportion of students currently studying is the same for both genders.


## Observed Data

teen_table <- matrix(
  c(3, 33,
    27, 9),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(teen_table) <- c("Men", "Women")
colnames(teen_table) <- c("Studying", "Not studying")

teen_table
```

### Chi-squared Test

```{r}
chisq_result <- chisq.test(teen_table)
chisq_result
```

#### Interpretation

The p-value is extremely small (less than 0.05), so we reject the null hypothesis of independence. This suggests a significant association between gender and study status.

### Fisher's Exact Test

```{r}
fisher_result <- fisher.test(teen_table)
fisher_result
```

#### Interpretation

The Fisher’s exact test also gives a very small p-value. Therefore, we again reject the null hypothesis and conclude that study status differs significantly by gender.

### Comparison of the Two Tests

-   The chi-squared test uses an approximation and performs best for larger samples [@agresti2018].
-   Fisher’s exact test calculates exact probabilities and is more suitable for small samples [@fisher1922].
-   The analysis was performed using R [@R-base] and dplyr [@dplyr].

### Simulation Study

To investigate whether Fisher’s exact test is conservative, a simulation study with 10,000 repetitions was conducted under four settings.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

set.seed(2026)

simulate_tests <- function(n_men, n_women, p, iterations = 10000) {

  results <- data.frame(
    chi_p = numeric(iterations),
    fisher_p = numeric(iterations)
  )

  for(i in 1:iterations){

    valid <- FALSE

    while(!valid){

      men_study <- rbinom(1, n_men, p)
      women_study <- rbinom(1, n_women, p)

      tab <- matrix(
        c(
          men_study,
          n_men - men_study,
          women_study,
          n_women - women_study
        ),
        nrow = 2,
        byrow = TRUE
      )

      valid <- all(rowSums(tab) > 0) & all(colSums(tab) > 0)
    }

    results$chi_p[i] <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab)$p.value)
    results$fisher_p[i] <- fisher.test(tab)$p.value
  }

  results
}

setting_1 <- simulate_tests(20,20,0.20)
setting_2 <- simulate_tests(20,20,0.50)
setting_3 <- simulate_tests(100,100,0.20)
setting_4 <- simulate_tests(100,100,0.50)

summarise_rejections <- function(results, setting_name){

  data.frame(
    Setting = setting_name,
    Test = c("Chi-squared test","Fisher's exact test"),

    Reject_10 = c(
      mean(results$chi_p < 0.10),
      mean(results$fisher_p < 0.10)
    ),

    Reject_5 = c(
      mean(results$chi_p < 0.05),
      mean(results$fisher_p < 0.05)
    ),

    Reject_1 = c(
      mean(results$chi_p < 0.01),
      mean(results$fisher_p < 0.01)
    )
  )
}

simulation_summary <- bind_rows(
  summarise_rejections(setting_1,"Setting 1: small sample, p = 0.20"),
  summarise_rejections(setting_2,"Setting 2: small sample, p = 0.50"),
  summarise_rejections(setting_3,"Setting 3: large sample, p = 0.20"),
  summarise_rejections(setting_4,"Setting 4: large sample, p = 0.50")
)

knitr::kable(
  simulation_summary,
  caption = "Simulation rejection rates for Chi-squared and Fisher's Exact Test"
)
```

### High Distinction Discussion

The simulation results suggest that Fisher's exact test can be conservative, especially in smaller sample settings. A conservative test rejects the null hypothesis less often than the nominal significance level.

For example, at the 5% significance level, if the Fisher rejection rate is below 0.05, this supports the statement that the actual rejection rate is below the nominal level.

The chi-squared test performs better when sample sizes are larger because its approximation becomes more accurate. Therefore, the simulation supports the claim that Fisher's exact test may be conservative in small-sample situations.

### Conclusion

Both tests detected a strong association in the observed dataset.

For small samples, Fisher’s exact test is recommended because it provides exact probabilities. For larger samples, the chi-squared test performs well and is computationally efficient.

The simulation confirms that Fisher’s exact test can be conservative, while the chi-squared test becomes more reliable with larger sample sizes.

### References

Agresti, A. (2018). *Statistical Methods for the Social Sciences*.

Wickham, H. et al. (2023). *dplyr Package Documentation*.

Fisher's Exact Test. Wikipedia.
